lesson.title: Trust Thyself: Transcendentalism and the American Mind
lesson.summary: A circle of New England writers built on the individualist spirit of the Great Awakening and the region's deep tradition of education to argue that truth came from personal intuition and nature, not institutions, reshaping American literature and reform.
lesson.body:
Transcendentalism emerged in New England in the 1830s as a reaction against the cool, rationalist Unitarian Christianity that dominated Harvard and Boston's educated elite. Unitarianism had itself been a reaction against the older Puritan Calvinism, but to a new generation of young ministers and writers it felt bloodless, too reliant on logical argument and historical evidence for religious belief and too little interested in direct spiritual experience. Transcendentalists argued instead that individuals could access truth directly through intuition, through communion with nature, and through the same kind of inner spiritual conviction that had once driven revivalists during the Great Awakening, even though the transcendentalists themselves were rarely conventionally religious.

This movement could only have taken the form it did in a region with New England's particular educational inheritance. The Puritan colonies had built an unusually literate society, founding Harvard College in 1636 and requiring towns to support schools so that colonists could read scripture for themselves. Transcendentalism, itself a movement built out of essays, lectures, and literary journals, depended on that long standing culture of reading, writing, and institutions like Harvard to produce both its authors and its audience, even as its leading figures reacted against the very rationalist education Harvard represented.

Ralph Waldo Emerson became the movement's central voice. A former Unitarian minister who resigned his pulpit in 1832, Emerson published the essay Nature in 1836, arguing that individuals should experience the divine directly through the natural world rather than through secondhand doctrine, and followed it in 1841 with Self Reliance, which urged readers to trust their own judgment over social convention and tradition. A loose group of like minded thinkers, sometimes called the Transcendental Club after they began meeting informally in 1836, gathered around Emerson, including the writer and editor Margaret Fuller, one of the era's most prominent female intellectuals.

Henry David Thoreau took these ideas furthest into practice. He spent just over two years living simply beside Walden Pond near Concord, Massachusetts, an experiment he turned into the 1854 book Walden, and in 1846 he spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax as a protest against slavery and the Mexican American War, an act of principled lawbreaking he explained in his influential 1849 essay Civil Disobedience. Some transcendentalists took their idealism into communal living as well, founding the utopian Brook Farm community outside Boston in 1841, which lasted until a fire and financial troubles ended it in 1847.

Transcendentalism's insistence that individual conscience outranked law or custom gave moral force to the era's reform movements, including abolitionism, and it produced a body of literature that gave the young United States its first distinctly American voice in philosophy and letters, rather than one borrowed wholesale from Europe.
